questions.q: What is withholding tax, in the context of Accounts Payable?
options: A discount the supplier voluntarily offers for early payment
A legally required deduction from a supplier payment, remitted to a tax authority
A fee charged by the bank for processing a payment
An optional surcharge an organization can add to any invoice
questions.explain: Withholding tax is a legal obligation: part of the payment goes to a tax authority instead of the supplier, driven by supplier-level setup.

questions.q: In the Harbor Point Logistics example, a $10,000 invoice is subject to 10% withholding. How much is actually paid to the supplier?
questions.explain: $10,000 minus the $1,000 withheld leaves $9,000 paid directly to the supplier; the $1,000 is remitted to the tax authority.

questions.q: What is retainage designed to do?
options: Calculate sales tax on an invoice
Hold back a percentage of progress payments as leverage until a contract is fully complete
Replace the need for a purchase order on service contracts
Automatically convert an invoice to a different currency
questions.explain: Retainage withholds a percentage of each progress payment until the contracted work is finished and accepted.

questions.q: What kind of purchase order is retainage typically set up on?
options: A standard PO for office supplies
A blanket agreement with no billing schedule
A complex (progress-payment) PO billed across multiple invoices over time
A two-way matched PO for a single delivery
questions.explain: Retainage applies to complex, progress-payment purchase orders where a contract is billed in stages rather than as one invoice.

questions.q: What releases accumulated retainage back to the contractor?
options: A retainage release invoice, created once the contract is complete and accepted
A credit memo from the supplier
Retainage is never released -- it is permanently withheld
questions.explain: A retainage release invoice pays out the amount withheld across progress invoices once the work passes final acceptance.
